replacement: Many people in Europe tend to believe without saying so, or to say without believing, that one of the great advantages of universal suffrage is that it puts the direction of public affairs in the hands of men who deserve the public’s confidence. They admit that the people cannot govern itself, but they assert that it is always sincerely disposed to promote the welfare of the state, and that it instinctively picks out those who share its good intentions and are best fit to hold supreme authority. I confess that what I observed in America does not agree with these opinions at all. When I arrived in the United States I was surprised to find so much distinguished talent among the governed and so little among the heads of the government. It is a well-established fact that today the ablest men in the United States are very rarely placed at the head of affairs, and it must be acknowledged that this has come about as democracy has overstepped all its former limits. The breed of American statesmen has clearly declined remarkably over the last fifty years.

note: Capitalized State used for the political body, against the style note.
replacement: Another cause tends to make the efforts of a democratic government less persevering than those of an aristocracy. The lower classes are not only less alert than the higher orders to the good or bad chances of the future, but they also suffer far more keenly from present privations. The nobleman does risk his life, but the chance of glory is as great as the chance of harm. If he gives up a large part of his income to the state, he deprives himself for a time of the pleasures of wealth. But for the poor man, death is adorned with no pomp or renown, and the taxes that are irksome to the rich are fatal to him.

note: Capitalized State used for the political body, against the style note.
replacement: Nothing is more embarrassing in the ordinary course of life than this irritable patriotism of the Americans. A stranger may be quite willing to praise many of the institutions of their country, but he asks permission to criticize some of the peculiarities he observes, and that permission is firmly refused. America is therefore a free country in which, lest anyone be hurt by your remarks, you are not allowed to speak freely of private individuals or of the state, of the citizens or of the authorities, of public or of private undertakings, or in short of anything at all, except the climate and the soil. And even then Americans will be found ready to defend one or the other, as if the inhabitants of the country had designed them.
